title: Why a vote needs to stay sealed
excerpts: You need to commit to a value without revealing it, then reveal it later.
A teacher needs to grade without seeing the exam first.
A bidder needs to submit a sealed bid.

title: What is a commitment
excerpts: A cryptographic commitment seals a value: commit(value) → commitment.
Later, you can open it to reveal the original value.
Properties: hiding (can't see value) and binding (can't change value).

codeBlocks.title: Commitment concept

title: The two properties
excerpts: Hiding - the commitment doesn't reveal the value.
Binding - once committed, you can't change what you committed to.
These make commitments fundamental to privacy protocols.

title: Commitments in Midnight
excerpts: Midnight provides two primitives: persistentCommit and persistentHash.
These are stored in the ledger.
They are the foundation for private data handling.

title: persistentCommit: the sealed value
excerpts: persistentCommit stores a value that can only be revealed by the holder of the opening key.
Like a safe deposit box - only the owner can open it.
Perfect for vote encryption and token amounts.

codeBlocks.title: persistentCommit

title: persistentHash: the public fingerprint
excerpts: persistentHash is a public commitment - a fingerprint of a value.
Anyone can compute it but can't reverse it.
Useful for public data that needs integrity verification.

codeBlocks.title: persistentHash

title: When to use each
excerpts: Use persistentCommit for values that must remain hidden until revealed.
Use persistentHash for data that's public but needs integrity.
The choice affects privacy.

title: The opening key
excerpts: persistentCommit uses commitment + opening key.
Only someone with the opening key can reveal the value.
This enables selective disclosure.

title: Why the register must stay protected
excerpts: You need to prove something belongs to a set without listing all members.
How do you prove you belong to the electoral register without revealing who you are?
Merkle trees solve this efficiently.

title: What is a Merkle tree
excerpts: A binary tree where each leaf is a hash of data.
Each parent is the hash of its children's hashes.
The root is a compact representation of all data.

codeBlocks.title: Merkle tree structure
codeBlocks.code:
Leaves: [hash(A), hash(B), hash(C), hash(D)]
Parents: [hash(hash(A)+hash(B)), hash(hash(C)+hash(D))]
Root: hash(hash(A,B) + hash(C,D))

title: Merkle proof of membership
excerpts: Provide leaf value + sibling hashes along path to root.
Verifier recomputes the root from these.
Proof size is O(log n) - efficient for large sets.

codeBlocks.title: Merkle proof verification

title: Using Merkle trees in circuits
excerpts: Verify Merkle proofs in a circuit.
Circuit takes leaf, proof path, and recomputes root.
Prove membership without revealing which element you are.

title: Application: verifiable electoral register
excerpts: The election authority publishes a Merkle root of the eligible register.
Each citizen proves membership using a Merkle proof in a ZK circuit.
Verify eligibility without revealing identity.

title: Application: token balance verification
excerpts: Commitments represent token amounts.
Merkle tree stores commitment openings.
Verify sufficient balance without revealing exact amount.

codeBlocks.title: Balance proof

title: The full flow
excerpts: 1. Commit to value with persistentCommit.
2. Store commitment in ledger.
3. For verification, use ZK circuit with Merkle proof.
4. Verifier checks commitment + proof without seeing values.

title: Putting it together
excerpts: Commitments and Merkle trees are the backbone of privacy on Midnight.
They enable proving properties about private data while keeping it hidden.
Master these, and you can build any private application.
